blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 25 (Organic Synthesis), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Explain the role of functional groups in organic synthesis. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Functional group: the part of an organic compound where most of the reactions occur.
2. Organic chemistry is organized around functional groups: millions of organic compounds are known, but there are only a handful of functional groups, and each one defines a family of organic compounds.
3. In organic synthesis we design different possible ways to build a target molecule from simpler, easily available components. Functional groups play a central role in designing such a synthesis.
4. They enable chemists to predict and control the reactions which ultimately lead to the desired product.
5. Identifying a functional group helps to predict the properties of a compound. This is crucial for developing new organic products and for ensuring the purity and composition of products such as medicines and food additives.

book_ref.quote: In organic synthesis we design different possible ways to build a target molecule from simpler easily available components.

blocks.prompt: 2 What points must be considered when planning the synthesis of an organic compound? Describe the two categories of reactions used in organic synthesis. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Points to consider:
• Before preparing an organic compound we must understand the chemical reactions, the reagents and the conditions required to complete each step, to guarantee successful formation of the target molecule.
• Most organic compounds can be prepared by a number of different routes, so criteria are needed to select the best route.
• A good synthesis converts cheap and easily available starting materials into the product by a route with the least number of steps and a high overall yield.

Categories of reactions:
1. Functional group interconversions (FGI): one functional group is converted into another.
2. Carbon-carbon bond formation: these are particularly important because the basic strategy of synthesis is to assemble the target molecule from simple and smaller starting materials.

book_ref.quote: Most organic compounds can be prepared by a number of different routes

blocks.prompt: 3 What is synthesis? Explain with equations how a primary aliphatic amine can be prepared in one step from a haloalkane and in two steps from an alcohol. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Synthesis: the target molecule is prepared starting from simple commercially available compounds. It may involve many steps or transformations to reach the final target molecule.

One step (from a haloalkane): the haloalkane is heated with excess ammonia dissolved in ethanol in a sealed tube (under pressure).
R–CH₂–Cl + NH₃ → R–CH₂–NH₂ + HCl
(CCl₄ is not the condition; ammonia hardly dissolves in it.)

Two steps (from an alcohol): a haloalkane is not easily available, so it is prepared from an alcohol, which is more easily available as a starting material.
Step 1: R–CH₂–OH → (SOCl₂) R–CH₂–Cl
Step 2: R–CH₂–Cl → (NH₃) R–CH₂–NH₂ + HCl

book_ref.quote: For example, primary aliphatic amine can be prepared in a single step

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe retrosynthesis and the disconnection approach. Which bonds are disconnected, and how is the route then used for synthesis? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Retrosynthesis is exactly the opposite of synthesis. The target molecule is broken down into less complicated, simpler and more readily available compounds which can serve as starting materials.
2. It involves the disconnection approach: the imaginary breaking down of the TM progressively into simpler starting materials. Each step is shown with the open retrosynthetic arrow ⇒.
3. Bonds chosen: those bonds of the target molecule are disconnected that result in a considerable structural simplification.
4. Disconnection gives synthons (often ionic fragments). Being usually unstable, they are replaced by synthetic equivalents (real reagents), which must be able to react to give the target molecule.
5. Following a series of disconnections we eventually arrive at simple, easily available starting materials. The synthesis is then carried out in the forward direction (→), from these starting materials to the target molecule (Figure 25.1).

book_ref.quote: In retrosynthesis, those bonds of the target molecule are disconnected

blocks.prompt: 5 Explain the following terms used in retrosynthesis, giving an example from the chapter where possible: (i) target molecule (ii) disconnection (iii) synthon (iv) synthetic equivalent (v) retrosynthetic tree. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Target molecule (TM): the molecule which is to be prepared, e.g. ethyl acetate, aniline, paracetamol.
(ii) Disconnection: the imaginary breaking down of the TM progressively into simpler starting materials, shown by the open-ended retrosynthetic arrow ⇒; e.g. disconnecting nitrobenzene at the C–N bond.
(iii) Synthon: a fragment of the target molecule generated by a disconnection. Synthons are often ionic species and are the building blocks for the synthesis, e.g. C₆H₅⁻ (aryl anion) and NO₂⁺ (nitronium cation).
(iv) Synthetic equivalent (SE): a reagent used to carry out the function of a synthon, which cannot itself be used because it is usually unstable, e.g. benzene for C₆H₅⁻ and nitric acid for NO₂⁺.
(v) Retrosynthetic tree: a diagram showing all possible disconnections and synthons from the target molecule to the starting materials (Figure 25.2 shows all the terms in one scheme).

book_ref.quote: Figure 25.2 shows all the terminologies in a single scheme.

blocks.prompt: 6 What is functional group interconversion (FGI)? Explain its role in designing synthetic routes, with two examples of FGI taken from the retrosyntheses in this chapter. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
FGI: the conversion of one functional group into another functional group, required for the synthesis of a specific compound, to reach the target molecule.

Role:
• FGI has a crucial role in designing routes which lead to target molecules.
• Using FGI as building blocks, simple starting materials can be converted into more complex target molecules.
• FGI not only allows the carbon skeleton of the target molecule to be created but also helps select the route to be adopted.
• The interconversions studied in earlier chapters are summarized in Figure 25.3 (aliphatic) and Figure 25.4 (aromatic).

Examples:
1. Aniline ⇒ nitrobenzene: –NH₂ is changed to –NO₂, because a nitro group is easily attached to benzene by electrophilic substitution, unlike an amino group by nucleophilic substitution.
2. 4-Aminophenol ⇒ 4-nitrophenol (paracetamol route): p-nitrophenol is easy to prepare and can then be reduced to p-aminophenol.

book_ref.quote: FGI is a phenomenon to change a functional group into another functional group

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain the retrosynthesis of ethyl acetate, naming the synthons and synthetic equivalents, and then give its synthesis with the equation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Target molecule: ethyl acetate, CH₃COOC₂H₅.

Step I, disconnection: the TM is disconnected at the indicated ester bond (CH₃CO–OC₂H₅), giving synthon A (CH₃CO⁺) and synthon B (C₂H₅O⁻).
Step II, synthetic equivalents: neutralizing the synthons gives acetic acid (for synthon A) and ethanol (for synthon B). These are simpler starting materials, and they can react to give the target molecule, which is the condition for choosing them.

Synthesis: a very familiar esterification reaction between acetic acid and ethanol, catalysed by H₂SO₄:
CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → (H₂SO₄) CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

book_ref.quote: For our target molecule ethyl acetate, the disconnection followed by neutralization yields acetic acid and ethanol

blocks.prompt: 8 Explain step by step the retrosynthetic analysis of aniline, giving the reason for each step. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Target molecule: aniline, C₆H₅–NH₂.

Step I, functional group interconversion: aniline ⇒ nitrobenzene. The amino group (–NH₂) is converted into the nitro group (–NO₂). Reason: it is easy to attach a nitro group on benzene by electrophilic substitution, rather than an amino group by nucleophilic substitution.

Step II, disconnection: nitrobenzene is disconnected at the C–N bond, creating the synthons aryl anion (C₆H₅⁻) and nitronium cation (NO₂⁺).

Step III, synthetic equivalents: the synthons are unstable, so they are neutralized to their synthetic equivalents, benzene (for C₆H₅⁻) and nitric acid (for NO₂⁺).

Thus the simple starting materials for aniline are benzene and nitric acid.

book_ref.quote: In second step the disconnection of nitrobenzene was done from C—N bond

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the retrosynthesis of acetophenone and design its synthesis. Name the process and the catalyst. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Target molecule: acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃.

Step I, disconnection: the TM is disconnected at the C–C bond between the ring and the acyl group, creating the synthons aryl anion (C₆H₅⁻) and acylium cation (CH₃CO⁺).
Step II, synthetic equivalents: neutralizing the synthons gives benzene (for C₆H₅⁻) and acyl chloride, CH₃COCl (for CH₃CO⁺).

Synthesis: benzene reacts with acyl chloride in the presence of AlCl₃ as catalyst. The process is Friedel-Craft acylation.
C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl → (AlCl₃) C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl

Here the disconnection of a C–C bond in retrosynthesis corresponds to a C–C bond formation reaction in synthesis.

book_ref.quote: In first step the disconnection of acetophenone (TM) was done from C—C bond

blocks.prompt: 10 Explain the reasoning behind each choice made in the retrosynthesis of paracetamol: why the amide C–N bond is disconnected first, why FGI is used, and what the final disconnection gives. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Why the amide C–N bond first (Steps I-II): paracetamol is disconnected at the C–N bond of its amide group. The synthetic equivalents of the resulting synthons, 4-aminophenol and acyl chloride, are well known to react through a nucleophilic addition-elimination reaction, so the amide can be rebuilt easily.

2. Why FGI (Step III): 4-aminophenol ⇒ 4-nitrophenol. This is done because p-nitrophenol is easy to prepare and can then be reduced to p-aminophenol. In retrosynthesis this FGI takes the open retrosynthetic arrow ⇒.

3. Final disconnection (Steps IV-V): 4-nitrophenol is disconnected at the C–N bond, giving the 4-hydroxy aryl anion (HO–C₆H₄⁻) and the nitronium cation (NO₂⁺). Their synthetic equivalents are phenol and nitric acid.

4. Result: the complex drug is traced back to phenol, a simple starting material. Synthesis then runs forward: phenol → 4-nitrophenol → 4-aminophenol → paracetamol.

book_ref.quote: The bond is broken at the position indicated because the synthetic equivalents

blocks.prompt: 11 Both aspirin and paracetamol are synthesized starting from phenol. Compare their retrosynthetic routes step by step. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both drugs look complex, but proper disconnections trace each back to phenol as the simple starting material. The routes compare as follows:

book_ref.quote: Aspirin and Paracetamol, both are synthesized starting from phenol.

rows: Step I: disconnection at the C–N bond of the amide group
Step I: disconnection at the C–O bond of the ester linkage
Step II: SE are 4-aminophenol and acyl chloride (they react by nucleophilic addition-elimination)
Step II: SE are salicylic acid and acetic anhydride
Step III: FGI 4-aminophenol ⇒ 4-nitrophenol (easy to prepare, then reduced)
Step III: Disconnection-II at the C–C bond of the carboxylic group
Steps IV-V: C–N disconnection of 4-nitrophenol gives HO–C₆H₄⁻ + NO₂⁺; SE phenol and nitric acid
Step IV: SE phenol and carbon dioxide
Starting materials: phenol, nitric acid, acyl chloride
Starting materials: phenol, carbon dioxide, acetic anhydride

blocks.prompt: 12 Explain why retrosynthesis is important in the synthesis of pharmaceutical products, using the examples of paracetamol and aspirin. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. One of the most important applications of retrosynthesis is in pharmaceutical product synthesis.
2. Hundreds of valuable medicinal compounds look very complex in structure, but if they are disconnected properly and efficiently, they lead back to very simple and commonly available starting materials. This is the beauty of organic synthesis: a complex, terrifying structure looks simple and achievable after a series of efficient retrosynthetic steps.
3. Paracetamol: its direct synthesis requires a series of steps; this series is decoded by its retrosynthesis (C–N disconnection, FGI to 4-nitrophenol, C–N disconnection), which leads back to phenol and nitric acid.
4. Aspirin: retrosynthesis shows how many and which steps are actually needed to prepare aspirin from phenol (C–O disconnection of the ester to salicylic acid and acetic anhydride, then C–C disconnection to phenol and carbon dioxide).
5. So retrosynthesis tells which reactions, in which order, are needed to reach the drug from simple starting materials.

book_ref.quote: There are hundreds of valuable medicinal compounds, which look very complex in their structure

blocks.prompt: 13 Describe how artificial intelligence was used by researchers at MIT to discover halicin. What problem was it meant to solve? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Problem: very few new antibiotics have been developed in the past few decades, and those are only slightly different from existing ones. Current methods are very costly, time consuming and limited to a narrow spectrum of chemical activity, and pathogens (bacteria) are becoming resistant to the prevalent antibiotics.

Use of AI:
1. Researchers at MIT designed a machine-learning algorithm to look for chemical features that make molecules effective at killing E. coli bacteria.
2. The model was applied on 2500 molecules and a set of 800 natural products with different structures and a wide range of bioactivities.
3. It picked out one molecule predicted to have antibacterial properties, with a molecular structure different from the existing antibiotics.
4. A different model showed that this molecule would most likely show low toxicity to human cells.
5. The molecule was named halicin. Tested against bacterial strains isolated from patients, it killed many of the world's most problematic disease-causing bacteria which were previously resistant to treatment.

book_ref.quote: In order to find out a solution to this problem the researchers at MIT

blocks.prompt: 14 After identifying halicin, how was the computer model used further? Why is this work called groundbreaking? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Further use of the model:
1. The researchers applied their computer model to screen more than 100 million molecules selected from a database.
2. The screening was completed in only three days.
3. It selected 23 more molecules with structures different from existing antibiotics.
4. Eight of these molecules showed antibacterial activities, and two were particularly powerful.

Why groundbreaking: ordinary drug-development methods are very costly, time consuming and limited to a narrow spectrum of chemical activity. Screening millions of molecules in days, and finding new structures unlike existing antibiotics, points out an altogether different route to discover new organic molecules which may be used as drugs.

book_ref.quote: This groundbreaking work points out an altogether different route to discover new organic molecules
